content: Pulsatile insulin refers to the administration of insulin in discrete pulses rather than as a continuous infusion. This method of delivery is designed to replicate the natural secretion of insulin by the pancreas into the portal vein, which subsequently drains into the liver. In healthy, non-diabetic individuals, the pancreas secretes insulin in response to food intake, with the amount of insulin released varying based on the quantity of food consumed. Essentially, the more food ingested, the greater the insulin secretion, among other influencing factors. Experimental evidence strongly suggests that pulsatile insulin has a more pronounced hypoglycemic effect compared to continuous insulin infusion. Continuous exposure to insulin and glucagon is known to reduce the metabolic effectiveness of these hormones on glucose production in humans, as the body develops an increased tolerance to their effects. This phenomenon may be partially explained by cellular-level downregulation, which diminishes the action of steady-state insulin levels. In contrast, pulsatile hormone secretion may allow for the recovery of receptor affinity and receptor numbers for insulin. Intermittent intravenous insulin administration, characterized by peaks in insulin concentrations, may enhance the suppression of gluconeogenesis and reduce hepatic glucose production. Dr. Thomas Aoki, a former Head of Metabolism Research at the Joslin Diabetes Center in Boston and a current Professor of Medicine at the University of California, Davis, was a pioneer in the use of pulsatile insulin for the treatment of diabetes. Dr. Aoki’s research emphasized the role of liver dysfunction in diabetic metabolism. He hypothesized that end-organ damage in diabetes is caused by abnormal hepatic glucose metabolism, insufficient insulin delivery, and insulin resistance. Under normal physiological conditions, insulin is secreted by the pancreas in pulses into the portal vein, which delivers blood to the liver in variable amounts, closely linked to meal ingestion. Hepatocytes require specific insulin levels (200–500 µU/mL in the portal vein) in conjunction with elevated glucose levels to activate key hepatic enzymes such as glucokinase, phosphofructokinase, and pyruvate kinase. In non-diabetic individuals, portal insulin concentrations are two to three times higher than those in the peripheral circulation. During the first pass through the liver, approximately 50% of the insulin is removed, strongly indicating that the liver is the primary metabolic target organ of the gastrointestinal tract and pancreas. The insulin retained by hepatocytes may be critical for the long-term effects of insulin on hepatic glucose metabolism, growth, and de novo enzyme synthesis. Following oral glucose intake, the liver accounts for an equal or greater proportion of total net glucose uptake compared to peripheral tissues. Insulin plays a pivotal role in controlling glucose levels by directly or indirectly regulating hepatic glucose production. In diabetic patients, a relative deficiency of insulin at the hepatocyte level impairs the liver’s ability to process incoming dietary glucose. Given the liver’s role as the target organ of the pancreas, the goal of administering pulsatile insulin to diabetic patients should extend beyond merely controlling blood glucose levels to include the normalization of hepatic metabolism. Furthermore, the hepatic enzymes influenced by insulin are also present in all glucose-utilizing bodily systems, suggesting a synchronized effect of insulin and glucose. It has been demonstrated that diabetic patients have a significantly impaired capacity to oxidize and store exogenous carbohydrates. In contrast, non-diabetic individuals exhibit an increase in respiratory quotient (RQ) and CO2 production after glucose administration, indicating that glucose has become the primary energy source. However, in diabetic patients on conventional insulin therapy, no such increase in RQ or CO2 production is observed. Liver and muscle tissues appear to be the most active in glucose oxidation. Studies have shown that resting muscle is not the source of increased CO2 production after glucose ingestion in non-diabetic individuals. It is postulated that achieving and maintaining hepatic activation in diabetic patients through pulsatile insulin treatment could reduce the frequency of hypoglycemic reactions.
